Figure 4.3: scRNA-seq prediction performance. (A) Distribution of predicted marker gene expression vs. ground truth across cell types showed great consistency and cell type specificity. (B) UMAP of actual scRNA-seq colored by actual and predicted gene expression values for the marker genes showed close resemblance. (C) normalized mean actual vs. predicted expression values captured cell type-specific variations.
We included the publicly available human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) 10k dataset and brain prefrontal cortex (PFC) dataset with parallel scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq sequencing to test our model. During the training process, we ignored the shared barcode to mimic the unpaired single-cell data, while we use the linking information as ground truth in our evaluation processes. For all modalities, we first extracted counts using CellRangerarc (version 2.0.2) with hg38 and default parameters (see detailed preprocessing steps in supplementary methods).
scRNA-seq pre-processing. We filtered out cells with insufficient reads ( < 200) or possi- ble multiplets [95] and kept the top 3,000 highly variable genes to form the scRNA-seq matrix using Pegasus (version 1.7.1) and Doubletdetection (version 4.2). We then conducted lognormalization on the entire matrix to yield the final matrix for training. We also conducted LEIDEN clustering [255] based on the PCA results (20 dimensions) and annotated their cell types using previously-studied marker genes.
scATAC-seq pre-processing. Similarly, we filtered out cells with insufficient TSS enrichment ( < 2 . 0), poor sequencing depths ( < 1000), or possible multiplets using ArchR (version 1.0.1) and default parameters otherwise [103]. The peaks were called using Macs2 (version 2.2.9.1) [296] and underwent TF-IDF algorithm [210] such that only the most informative 100,000 peaks were kept. Finally, the binarized matrix was used in the training and evaluation process. To generate the cell type annotation for the discriminator, LEIDEN clustering based on the LSI results (top 20 dimension) were also used and the gene activity scores.
Summary of data used in this study. Previously, we downloaded deeply sequenced scATAC-seq and scRNA-seq co-assayed data from three frozen PFC tissues (GSE216270). After strict QC, we kept 27,414 barcodes from 5 samples with seven major cell types (excitatory, inhibitory, astrocytes, endothelial, microglia, oligodendrocytes, and OPC) using the set of marker genes proposed by Lake et al. [148].
We also use the publicly available human peripheral blood mono-nuclear cells (PBMC) 10k dataset from the 10x Genomics website. We kept 11,582 cells from 28 cell types as suggested on the website. Cell type annotations were adopted from the Signac vignettes [239].

GRIDS: Learnable Subset Perturbations for Global Regulatory Redundancy Reasoning
5.3 Methods
5.3.1 Problem Setup
Following the formulation in Wu et al. [273], we represent the cis-regulatory landscape of a cell by an ATAC-seq vector x ∈ { 0 , 1 } d a , where each entry corresponds to the accessibility state of a genomic peak (1 for open and 0 for closed). In practice, ATAC-seq profiles are extremely high-dimensional, typically with d a > 10 5 . The corresponding gene expression measurements (RNA-seq) are denoted by a real-valued vector y ∈ R d r , where d a and d r indicate the numbers of peaks and genes, respectively.
Asingle-cell multi-omics dataset is given as a collection of N paired multi-modal observations C = { c (1) , c (2) , . . . , c ( N ) } , where each cell c ( i ) = ( x ( i ) , y ( i ) ) consists of an ATAC-seq profile x ( i ) and its matched RNA-seq profile y ( i ). In addition, each cell c ( i ) is associated with a semantic label ℓ ( i ) ∈ { 1 , . . . , T } indicating its cell type among T classes. For a given cell type T = k , we denote by C k the subset of C containing all cells whose labels satisfy ℓ ( i ) = k .
As introduced above, gene expression is regulated through CRE-mediated transcriptional control implemented by complex intracellular processes. We abstract this relationship using a regulatory function y = F ( x ), where F ( x ) : R d a → R d r . Because F corresponds to an underlying biological mechanism, it is costly to query directly and is treated as a black box. The regulatory redundancy dissection problem then aims to identify a subset of L peak indices r = { r 1 , . . . , r L } within the CRE space (i.e., the subset feature in the ATAC-seq x r ≡ { x j | j ∈ r } ) that are crucial for controlling a target gene's expression over a population of cells. The search domain of r is the binomial subset space ( d a L ) , which is prohibitively large given that x typically contains more than 10 5 dimensions.
To make this problem tractable, we model redundancy dissection within a global feature explanation framework. In general, global explanations quantify how much a model's performance degrades over a sample population when selected features are removed [46]. Under the regulatory redundancy setting, the corresponding global objective can be written as

where L measures the expected degradation in gene expression. Here, x \ r denotes the perturbed CRE representation induced by r , obtained by replacing the original features x r j with preset perturbation values p ∈ R d a at the indices specified by r (i.e., x \ r,r j = p r j ). When p = 0, this reduces to a removal-based perturbation. The specific form of the loss depends on the model and task [63]; for instance, cross-entropy is commonly used to measure probability degradation in classification, whereas in our setting we adopt a mean-squared loss to quantify degradation of gene expression values. The optimal subset r ∗ in Eq. 1 corresponds to the solution of the regulatory redundancy problem described above.

GRIDS: Learnable Subset Perturbations for Global Regulatory Redundancy Reasoning
5.3 Methods
5.3.5 Evaluation Metrics
Single-Cell Multimodal Dataset. We curated a deeply sequenced single-cell multimodal dataset from postmortem human PFC [79, 5]. The dataset contains N = 10 , 266 cells spanning T = 8 cell types, with each cell profiled for both chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) and transcriptional activity (RNA-seq). On the ATAC-seq modality, we called d a = 127 , 219 peaks using Macs2 [296], and the average sequencing depth (i.e., the number of open states per cell) is 4811 . 34. For RNA-seq, we applied standard quality control and preprocessing using the default parameters recommended by Pegasus [154], and retained d r = 3000 genes. Additional dataset details are provided in Appendix D.2. We evaluate GRIDS by learning global feature subsets r of varying sequence length L for multiple target genes, using masking-based perturbations on the CRE input with p = 0. In each experiment, we randomly split the full dataset into training, validation, and test sets with ratios 0 . 7, 0 . 1, and 0 . 2, respectively. Global explanations are learned on the training set and evaluated on the held-out test set. Hyperparameter settings are reported in Appendix D.3.
MNIST Dataset. To further demonstrate the ability of GRIDS to recover combinatorial feature effects, we performed additional experiments on binary digit classification using MNIST. We compared GRIDS with strong baselines under the same global explanation evaluation protocol. The full set of results is summarized in Appendix D.4, where we observe that GRIDS can effectively identify combinatorial features in the input space.

Disease-Driven Regulatory Rewiring with Multi-Omic and Spatial Validation
6.1 Introduction
Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is a prevalent psychiatric condition that can develop following exposure to severe traumatic events. In the general population, PTSD affects roughly 6-8% of individuals [183, 30]. Genetic studies indicate moderate heritability (approximately 24%-40%) [3], and large-scale association analyses support a highly polygenic architecture [237, 77, 96, 196]. Recent post-mortem investigations have started to clarify the molecular features of brains from individuals with PTSD [99, 166, 122, 69]. Work to date has largely centered on the prefrontal cortex (PFC) and amygdala, revealing alterations across multiple pathways, including GABAergic signalling, immunity and neuroinflammation, and glucocorticoid signalling. The breadth of implicated biological processes suggests that PTSD pathophysiology is unlikely to be attributable to a single cell type.
In the human brain, transcriptional programs are shaped by cis-regulatory elements (CREs) together with chromatin modifications and transcription factor binding at enhancers and promoters. Establishing which CREs are active in specific cell types is essential for understanding how disease-associated variants influence gene expression. Prior studies have reported robust PTSD-associated differences in DNA methylation [69, 155]; however, to our knowledge, the single-cell chromatin landscape of the brain has not been comprehensively characterized in PTSD. Advances in genomic profiling now make it possible to measure chromatin organization at single-cell resolution, and to pair these measurements with gene expression to pinpoint how risk variants modulate transcription within individual cellular contexts [219, 151, 185].
Here, we report a multi-omic study of over two million nuclei isolated from the dorsolateral PFC (DLPFC) spanning three diagnostic groups: individuals with major depressive disorder (MDD), individuals with PTSD, and control individuals with neither condition (CON). Using paired single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) and single-nucleus assay for transposase-accessible chromatin sequencing (snATAC-seq), we integrated transcriptomic and epigenomic profiles to annotate and quantify all major brain cell classes, including excitatory and inhibitory neurons as well as non-neuronal populations. This atlas enabled detection of cell-type-specific differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in PTSD and identification of both shared and distinct expression changes between PTSD and MDD. We additionally performed high-resolution single-cell spatial transcriptomics on tissue from 18 donors, which corroborated DEGs and revealed disrupted cell-to-cell communication (CCC) patterns involving somatostatin (SST) interneurons and microglia in PTSD. To link regulatory variation to transcriptional outcomes, we integrated RNA and ATAC modalities to define CREs, connect them to putative target genes, and fine-map eight credible risk loci within these candidate enhancers. We uncovered selective perturbations of the glucocorticoid system that were, unexpectedly, most prominent in endothelial cells. We further observed heightened vulnerability of SST interneurons in PTSD, alongside transcriptome-wide shifts consistent with reduced SST signalling and neurotransmission. Collectively, these results delineate pathway-level dynamics across diverse cortical cell types and provide predictions of cis-regulatory logic and associated factors that contribute to the molecular aetiology of PTSD.

ABSTRACT OF THE DISSERTATION
From Modality Translation to Regulatory Reasoning: Interpretable AI for Single-Cell Multi-Omic Systems
By
Siwei Xu
Doctor of Philosophy in Computer Science
University of California, Irvine, 2026
Associate Professor Jing Zhang, Chair
Single-cell and spatial multi-omic profiling boosts biological discoveries by measuring gene expression, chromatin state, and tissue context across substantial cellular and tissue heterogeneity; however, most studies remain partially observed: modalities are often missing or unpaired, measurements are sparse, and distributions shift across protocols and cohorts. These properties induce central computer-science challenges in robust representation learning, cross-modality translation under partial observability, and interpretable reasoning over high-dimensional regulatory mechanisms. This work develops learning and inference frameworks capable of modeling the scale and heterogeneity of consortium datasets, where close collaboration between computational and experimental scientists is essential to convert large cohort resources into reproducible analysis pipelines and robust, interpretable model outputs.
We first develop robust epigenetic representations and leverage them to construct a cohortscale brain genomic atlas. Translator learns reusable scATAC-seq chromatin representations from high-quality references. It uses transfer learning to adapt them to heterogeneous target datasets, improving robustness to sparsity and technical variation. Building on this foundation, we contribute to population-scale integration through the psychENCODE2 consortium, which enables a standardized computational pipeline for more than 2.8 million nuclei from 388 human prefrontal cortex donors. In this setting, consortium-scale hetero- geneity functions as a rigorous evaluation regime that surfaces real-world constraints for algorithm design, including cross-individual variability, batch effects, and the need for scalable harmonization. The resulting integrated resource supports cell-type-resolved regulatory features and network construction, and enables further downstream computational tasks at cohort scale.
Wethen address modality completion, cross-modal translation, and mechanistic interpretability. scACT learns cycle-consistent cross-modality mappings from unpaired single-cell data, enabling reliable multi-omic alignment and accurate translation while supporting perturbationbased probes of cross-modal correspondence. To advance from translation to explicit regulatory reasoning, GRIDS formulates combinatorial cis -regulation as a global explanation problem and introduces learnable subset perturbations to identify redundant sets of regulatory elements that jointly control gene programs. Finally, we demonstrate disease-scale discovery using a multimodal PTSD brain cohort with spatial validation, integrating transcriptomic, epigenomic, and spatial measurements to prioritize cell-type-specific regulatory programs and candidate mechanisms under strong biological and technical heterogeneity typical of large collaborative studies.
Together, these contributions establish a coherent computational pathway from robust representation learning to modality translation and interpretable regulatory reasoning, providing scalable methods that transform incomplete multi-omic measurements into reproducible in-silico experiments and testable regulatory hypotheses in consortium-scale human brain datasets.

6.2 Single-cell multi-omic analysis of the PFC in PTSD
To characterize cell-type-resolved transcriptional and regulatory alterations in PTSD (Fig. 6.1a), we generated snRNA-seq and snATAC-seq profiles from dorsolateral PFC (DLPFC) tissue collected from 111 donors. The cohort comprised 36 donors with PTSD, 36 donors with major depressive disorder (MDD; psychiatric control), and 39 control donors with neither diagnosis (CON) (Extended Data Fig. 1a). We present findings from a discovery dataset including 935,371 nuclei assayed by snRNA-seq (Fig. 6.1b and Supplementary Fig. 1), 473,033 nuclei assayed by snATAC-seq (Fig. 6.1c and Supplementary Fig. 2), and 119,431 nuclei profiled by single-nucleus multiome (snMultiome) (Fig. 6.1d and Supplementary Fig. 3). The snMultiome component provided direct pairing of barcoded mRNA and chromatin accessibility from the same nuclei. Four snMultiome samples overlapped with the discovery cohort (Extended Data Fig. 1b and Supplementary Table 1).
Across snRNA-seq, we annotated major cortical cell classes using established marker-gene expression (Extended Data Fig. 2d), including excitatory neurons (EXNs; four subtypes: CUX2, RORB, FEZF2, and OPRK1), inhibitory neurons (INs; five subtypes: LAMP5, KCNG1, VIP, SST, and PVALB), oligodendrocytes (OLGs), oligodendrocyte progenitor cells (OPCs), endothelial cells (ENDs), astrocytes (ASTs), and microglia (MG) (Fig. 6.1b and Extended Data Fig. 2a). Nuclei counts by cell type and modality are summarized in Supplementary Table 2. We quantified differential cell-type abundance using scCODA [36] based on nuclei numbers across modalities, and observed reduced OLG abundance (false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.05) in PTSD compared with both CON and MDD (Fig. 6.1b). Using snATAC-seq, we recovered the same seven canonical brain cell types (Fig. 6.1c and Extended Data Fig. 2b), supported by cell-type-specific accessibility at marker loci (Extended Data Fig. 2e), and obtained concordant annotations in snMultiome (Fig. 6.1d and Extended Data Fig. 2c). To resolve finer transcriptomic structure (Extended Data Fig. 2f), we leveraged prior subtype annotations [172] and identified 61 subtypes comprising 18 EXN subtypes, 30 IN subtypes, and 13 non-neuronal subtypes, including two OLG subtypes, three AST subtypes, macrophages, T cells (T SKAP1 CD247), smooth muscle cells, and pericytes (Extended Data Fig. 2f,g).

3.1 Introduction
To address this gap, the PsychENCODE Consortium generated single-cell sequencing data from adult brains with multiple neuropsychiatric disorders in the human prefrontal cortex, using single-nucleus (sn) assays for RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq), snATAC-seq (ATAC, assay for transposase-accessible chromatin), and snMultiome. Leveraging these data and integrating them with other published studies [26, 72, 262, 172], we created a uniformly processed single-cell resource at the population level. This resource, which we call brainSCOPE (brain single-cell omics for PsychENCODE), comprises > 2.8 million nuclei from 388 individual brains, including 333 newly generated samples and 55 from external sources (figs. S1 and S2). It enables us to assess 28 distinct brain cell types that can be registered against previously identified canonical cell types [26, 172]. Using the resource, we identified an average of 85,000 cis-eQTLs per cell type and 550,000 cell type-specific cis-regulatory elements, which were enriched for variants associated with brain-related disorders. Using our regulatory elements and eQTLs, we inferred cell type-specific gene regulatory networks (which show great changes across cell types) as well as cell-to-cell communication networks. Moreover, we precisely quantified expression variation in the population, finding, for instance, that common neurorelated drug targets such as CNR1 demonstrate a high degree of cell-type variability and low interindividual variability and that the transcriptomes of specific neurons are highly predictive of an individual's age. Lastly, we developed an integrative model to impute cell type-specific functional genomic information for individuals from genotype data alone. Using this model, we prioritized many known and some additional disease genes, now with information about their specific cell type of action. We further associated this prioritization with potential drug targets and simulated the effects of perturbing the expression of particular genes.
All sequencing data, derived analysis files, and computer codes are available from the brainSCOPE resource portal (brainscope.psychencode.org; figs. S3 to S5); these data include gene-expression matrices from snRNA-seq data, regulatory regions from snATAC-seq data, variability metrics for all genes, single-cell QTL callsets, regulatory and cell-to-cell communication networks, and the integrative model and its prioritization outputs.

5.3.1 Problem Setup
Following the formulation in Wu et al. [273], we represent the cis-regulatory landscape of a cell by an ATAC-seq vector x ∈ { 0 , 1 } d a , where each entry corresponds to the accessibility state of a genomic peak (1 for open and 0 for closed). In practice, ATAC-seq profiles are extremely high-dimensional, typically with d a > 10 5 . The corresponding gene expression measurements (RNA-seq) are denoted by a real-valued vector y ∈ R d r , where d a and d r indicate the numbers of peaks and genes, respectively.
Asingle-cell multi-omics dataset is given as a collection of N paired multi-modal observations C = { c (1) , c (2) , . . . , c ( N ) } , where each cell c ( i ) = ( x ( i ) , y ( i ) ) consists of an ATAC-seq profile x ( i ) and its matched RNA-seq profile y ( i ). In addition, each cell c ( i ) is associated with a semantic label ℓ ( i ) ∈ { 1 , . . . , T } indicating its cell type among T classes. For a given cell type T = k , we denote by C k the subset of C containing all cells whose labels satisfy ℓ ( i ) = k .

The corresponding gene expression measurements (RNA-seq) are denoted by a real-valued vector y ∈ R d r , where d a and d r indicate the numbers of peaks and genes, respectively.

We included the publicly available human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) 10k dataset and brain prefrontal cortex (PFC) dataset with parallel scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq sequencing to test our model. During the training process, we ignored the shared barcode to mimic the unpaired single-cell data, while we use the linking information as ground truth in our evaluation processes. For all modalities, we first extracted counts using CellRangerarc (version 2.0.2) with hg38 and default parameters (see detailed preprocessing steps in supplementary methods).

scRNA-seq pre-processing. We filtered out cells with insufficient reads ( < 200) or possi- ble multiplets [95] and kept the top 3,000 highly variable genes to form the scRNA-seq matrix using Pegasus (version 1.7.1) and Doubletdetection (version 4.2). We then conducted lognormalization on the entire matrix to yield the final matrix for training. We also conducted LEIDEN clustering [255] based on the PCA results (20 dimensions) and annotated their cell types using previously-studied marker genes.

scATAC-seq pre-processing. Similarly, we filtered out cells with insufficient TSS enrichment ( < 2 . 0), poor sequencing depths ( < 1000), or possible multiplets using ArchR (version 1.0.1) and default parameters otherwise [103]. The peaks were called using Macs2 (version 2.2.9.1) [296] and underwent TF-IDF algorithm [210] such that only the most informative 100,000 peaks were kept. Finally, the binarized matrix was used in the training and evaluation process. To generate the cell type annotation for the discriminator, LEIDEN clustering based on the LSI results (top 20 dimension) were also used and the gene activity scores.

Summary of data used in this study. Previously, we downloaded deeply sequenced scATAC-seq and scRNA-seq co-assayed data from three frozen PFC tissues (GSE216270). After strict QC, we kept 27,414 barcodes from 5 samples with seven major cell types (excitatory, inhibitory, astrocytes, endothelial, microglia, oligodendrocytes, and OPC) using the set of marker genes proposed by Lake et al. [148].

We also use the publicly available human peripheral blood mono-nuclear cells (PBMC) 10k dataset from the 10x Genomics website. We kept 11,582 cells from 28 cell types as suggested on the website. Cell type annotations were adopted from the Signac vignettes [239].

data_source_sections.text:
Single-Cell Multimodal Dataset. We curated a deeply sequenced single-cell multimodal dataset from postmortem human PFC [79, 5]. The dataset contains N = 10 , 266 cells spanning T = 8 cell types, with each cell profiled for both chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) and transcriptional activity (RNA-seq). On the ATAC-seq modality, we called d a = 127 , 219 peaks using Macs2 [296], and the average sequencing depth (i.e., the number of open states per cell) is 4811 . 34. For RNA-seq, we applied standard quality control and preprocessing using the default parameters recommended by Pegasus [154], and retained d r = 3000 genes. Additional dataset details are provided in Appendix D.2. We evaluate GRIDS by learning global feature subsets r of varying sequence length L for multiple target genes, using masking-based perturbations on the CRE input with p = 0. In each experiment, we randomly split the full dataset into training, validation, and test sets with ratios 0 . 7, 0 . 1, and 0 . 2, respectively. Global explanations are learned on the training set and evaluated on the held-out test set. Hyperparameter settings are reported in Appendix D.3.

MNIST Dataset. To further demonstrate the ability of GRIDS to recover combinatorial feature effects, we performed additional experiments on binary digit classification using MNIST. We compared GRIDS with strong baselines under the same global explanation evaluation protocol. The full set of results is summarized in Appendix D.4, where we observe that GRIDS can effectively identify combinatorial features in the input space.

Baseline Comparisons. We compare GRIDS with a collection of local and global featureimportance methods: (1) Random , a naive baseline that selects features uniformly at random for perturbation. (2) Saliency [230], a widely used gradient-based attribution method; we aggregate instance-wise saliency scores across samples to obtain global importance estimates. (3) LIME [212], a local explanation method that uses the submodular pick procedure to derive global feature importance from local explanations. (4) SmoothGrad [232], which samples noisy neighbors and estimates importance using averaged gradient-based saliency maps. (5) FIMAP [46], a neural-network-based approach that learns feature importance by finding minimal adversarial perturbations. (6) CXPlain [228], a global method that trains a surrogate explainer and perturbs features with predefined values to infer their importance. heading_path: Disease-Driven Regulatory Rewiring with Multi-Omic and Spatial Validation
data_source_sections.heading: 6.1 Introduction
data_source_sections.text:
Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is a prevalent psychiatric condition that can develop following exposure to severe traumatic events. In the general population, PTSD affects roughly 6-8% of individuals [183, 30]. Genetic studies indicate moderate heritability (approximately 24%-40%) [3], and large-scale association analyses support a highly polygenic architecture [237, 77, 96, 196]. Recent post-mortem investigations have started to clarify the molecular features of brains from individuals with PTSD [99, 166, 122, 69]. Work to date has largely centered on the prefrontal cortex (PFC) and amygdala, revealing alterations across multiple pathways, including GABAergic signalling, immunity and neuroinflammation, and glucocorticoid signalling. The breadth of implicated biological processes suggests that PTSD pathophysiology is unlikely to be attributable to a single cell type.

In the human brain, transcriptional programs are shaped by cis-regulatory elements (CREs) together with chromatin modifications and transcription factor binding at enhancers and promoters. Establishing which CREs are active in specific cell types is essential for understanding how disease-associated variants influence gene expression. Prior studies have reported robust PTSD-associated differences in DNA methylation [69, 155]; however, to our knowledge, the single-cell chromatin landscape of the brain has not been comprehensively characterized in PTSD. Advances in genomic profiling now make it possible to measure chromatin organization at single-cell resolution, and to pair these measurements with gene expression to pinpoint how risk variants modulate transcription within individual cellular contexts [219, 151, 185].

Here, we report a multi-omic study of over two million nuclei isolated from the dorsolateral PFC (DLPFC) spanning three diagnostic groups: individuals with major depressive disorder (MDD), individuals with PTSD, and control individuals with neither condition (CON). Using paired single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) and single-nucleus assay for transposase-accessible chromatin sequencing (snATAC-seq), we integrated transcriptomic and epigenomic profiles to annotate and quantify all major brain cell classes, including excitatory and inhibitory neurons as well as non-neuronal populations. This atlas enabled detection of cell-type-specific differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in PTSD and identification of both shared and distinct expression changes between PTSD and MDD. We additionally performed high-resolution single-cell spatial transcriptomics on tissue from 18 donors, which corroborated DEGs and revealed disrupted cell-to-cell communication (CCC) patterns involving somatostatin (SST) interneurons and microglia in PTSD. To link regulatory variation to transcriptional outcomes, we integrated RNA and ATAC modalities to define CREs, connect them to putative target genes, and fine-map eight credible risk loci within these candidate enhancers. We uncovered selective perturbations of the glucocorticoid system that were, unexpectedly, most prominent in endothelial cells. We further observed heightened vulnerability of SST interneurons in PTSD, alongside transcriptome-wide shifts consistent with reduced SST signalling and neurotransmission. Collectively, these results delineate pathway-level dynamics across diverse cortical cell types and provide predictions of cis-regulatory logic and associated factors that contribute to the molecular aetiology of PTSD.

data_source_sections.heading: ABSTRACT OF THE DISSERTATION
data_source_sections.text:
From Modality Translation to Regulatory Reasoning: Interpretable AI for Single-Cell Multi-Omic Systems

By

Siwei Xu

Doctor of Philosophy in Computer Science

University of California, Irvine, 2026

Associate Professor Jing Zhang, Chair

Single-cell and spatial multi-omic profiling boosts biological discoveries by measuring gene expression, chromatin state, and tissue context across substantial cellular and tissue heterogeneity; however, most studies remain partially observed: modalities are often missing or unpaired, measurements are sparse, and distributions shift across protocols and cohorts. These properties induce central computer-science challenges in robust representation learning, cross-modality translation under partial observability, and interpretable reasoning over high-dimensional regulatory mechanisms. This work develops learning and inference frameworks capable of modeling the scale and heterogeneity of consortium datasets, where close collaboration between computational and experimental scientists is essential to convert large cohort resources into reproducible analysis pipelines and robust, interpretable model outputs.

We first develop robust epigenetic representations and leverage them to construct a cohortscale brain genomic atlas. Translator learns reusable scATAC-seq chromatin representations from high-quality references. It uses transfer learning to adapt them to heterogeneous target datasets, improving robustness to sparsity and technical variation. Building on this foundation, we contribute to population-scale integration through the psychENCODE2 consortium, which enables a standardized computational pipeline for more than 2.8 million nuclei from 388 human prefrontal cortex donors. In this setting, consortium-scale hetero- geneity functions as a rigorous evaluation regime that surfaces real-world constraints for algorithm design, including cross-individual variability, batch effects, and the need for scalable harmonization. The resulting integrated resource supports cell-type-resolved regulatory features and network construction, and enables further downstream computational tasks at cohort scale.

Wethen address modality completion, cross-modal translation, and mechanistic interpretability. scACT learns cycle-consistent cross-modality mappings from unpaired single-cell data, enabling reliable multi-omic alignment and accurate translation while supporting perturbationbased probes of cross-modal correspondence. To advance from translation to explicit regulatory reasoning, GRIDS formulates combinatorial cis -regulation as a global explanation problem and introduces learnable subset perturbations to identify redundant sets of regulatory elements that jointly control gene programs. Finally, we demonstrate disease-scale discovery using a multimodal PTSD brain cohort with spatial validation, integrating transcriptomic, epigenomic, and spatial measurements to prioritize cell-type-specific regulatory programs and candidate mechanisms under strong biological and technical heterogeneity typical of large collaborative studies.

Together, these contributions establish a coherent computational pathway from robust representation learning to modality translation and interpretable regulatory reasoning, providing scalable methods that transform incomplete multi-omic measurements into reproducible in-silico experiments and testable regulatory hypotheses in consortium-scale human brain datasets.

data_source_sections.heading: 6.2 Single-cell multi-omic analysis of the PFC in PTSD
data_source_sections.text:
To characterize cell-type-resolved transcriptional and regulatory alterations in PTSD (Fig. 6.1a), we generated snRNA-seq and snATAC-seq profiles from dorsolateral PFC (DLPFC) tissue collected from 111 donors. The cohort comprised 36 donors with PTSD, 36 donors with major depressive disorder (MDD; psychiatric control), and 39 control donors with neither diagnosis (CON) (Extended Data Fig. 1a). We present findings from a discovery dataset including 935,371 nuclei assayed by snRNA-seq (Fig. 6.1b and Supplementary Fig. 1), 473,033 nuclei assayed by snATAC-seq (Fig. 6.1c and Supplementary Fig. 2), and 119,431 nuclei profiled by single-nucleus multiome (snMultiome) (Fig. 6.1d and Supplementary Fig. 3). The snMultiome component provided direct pairing of barcoded mRNA and chromatin accessibility from the same nuclei. Four snMultiome samples overlapped with the discovery cohort (Extended Data Fig. 1b and Supplementary Table 1).

Across snRNA-seq, we annotated major cortical cell classes using established marker-gene expression (Extended Data Fig. 2d), including excitatory neurons (EXNs; four subtypes: CUX2, RORB, FEZF2, and OPRK1), inhibitory neurons (INs; five subtypes: LAMP5, KCNG1, VIP, SST, and PVALB), oligodendrocytes (OLGs), oligodendrocyte progenitor cells (OPCs), endothelial cells (ENDs), astrocytes (ASTs), and microglia (MG) (Fig. 6.1b and Extended Data Fig. 2a). Nuclei counts by cell type and modality are summarized in Supplementary Table 2. We quantified differential cell-type abundance using scCODA [36] based on nuclei numbers across modalities, and observed reduced OLG abundance (false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.05) in PTSD compared with both CON and MDD (Fig. 6.1b). heading_path: psychENCODE2: Population-Scale Single-Cell Regulatory Systems and Modeling Constraints
data_source_sections.heading: 3.1 Introduction
data_source_sections.text:
Genetic variants linked to neuropsychiatric disorders affect brain functions on multiple levels, from gene expression in individual cells to complex brain circuits between cells [244, 208, 91]. At every level, they manifest themselves differently depending on the cell type in question. Previously, groups such as GTEx (Genotype-Tissue Expression), the PsychENCODE Consortium, and ROSMAP (Religious Orders Study and Memory and Aging Project) assembled cohorts large enough to link variants to their effects on gene expression in bulk tissue, generating comprehensive eQTL (expression quantitative trait locus) catalogs for the brain [263, 251, 193]. Although useful, these tissue-level results do not reflect the specific cell types involved; moreover, they do not provide strong evidence that eQTLs act in cell type-specific fashion [165, 32, 138, 290].

Recently, dramatic technological advances have allowed the measurement of gene expression and chromatin accessibility at the single-cell level [292, 26, 170]. The resulting datasets have shown that the brain has a particularly large number of distinct cell types; cell-type complexity is one of the brain's distinguishing features [26]. Many brain cell types have been rigorously defined, particularly by the Brain Research through Advancing Innovative Neurotechnologies (BRAIN) Initiative Cell Census Network (BICCN) [26, 291, 146]. Using these, we can potentially refine our understanding of how variants and gene regulation affect brain phenotypes, including neuropsychiatric disorders [233]. However, up to now we have not had sufficiently large cohorts, including a wide enough range of brain phenotypes, to make statistically meaningful associations between variants, regulatory elements, and expression and to develop comprehensive models of brain gene regulation at the single-cell level.

To address this gap, the PsychENCODE Consortium generated single-cell sequencing data from adult brains with multiple neuropsychiatric disorders in the human prefrontal cortex, using single-nucleus (sn) assays for RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq), snATAC-seq (ATAC, assay for transposase-accessible chromatin), and snMultiome. Leveraging these data and integrating them with other published studies [26, 72, 262, 172], we created a uniformly processed single-cell resource at the population level. This resource, which we call brainSCOPE (brain single-cell omics for PsychENCODE), comprises > 2.8 million nuclei from 388 individual brains, including 333 newly generated samples and 55 from external sources (figs. S1 and S2). It enables us to assess 28 distinct brain cell types that can be registered against previously identified canonical cell types [26, 172]. Using the resource, we identified an average of 85,000 cis-eQTLs per cell type and 550,000 cell type-specific cis-regulatory elements, which were enriched for variants associated with brain-related disorders. Using our regulatory elements and eQTLs, we inferred cell type-specific gene regulatory networks (which show great changes across cell types) as well as cell-to-cell communication networks. Moreover, we precisely quantified expression variation in the population, finding, for instance, that common neurorelated drug targets such as CNR1 demonstrate a high degree of cell-type variability and low interindividual variability and that the transcriptomes of specific neurons are highly predictive of an individual's age. Lastly, we developed an integrative model to impute cell type-specific functional genomic information for individuals from genotype data alone. Using this model, we prioritized many known and some additional disease genes, now with information about their specific cell type of action. We further associated this prioritization with potential drug targets and simulated the effects of perturbing the expression of particular genes.

All sequencing data, derived analysis files, and computer codes are available from the brainSCOPE resource portal (brainscope.psychencode.org; figs. S3 to S5); these data include gene-expression matrices from snRNA-seq data, regulatory regions from snATAC-seq data, variability metrics for all genes, single-cell QTL callsets, regulatory and cell-to-cell communication networks, and the integrative model and its prioritization outputs.

input_representation_sections.text:
Following the formulation in Wu et al. [273], we represent the cis-regulatory landscape of a cell by an ATAC-seq vector x ∈ { 0 , 1 } d a , where each entry corresponds to the accessibility state of a genomic peak (1 for open and 0 for closed). In practice, ATAC-seq profiles are extremely high-dimensional, typically with d a > 10 5 . The corresponding gene expression measurements (RNA-seq) are denoted by a real-valued vector y ∈ R d r , where d a and d r indicate the numbers of peaks and genes, respectively.

Asingle-cell multi-omics dataset is given as a collection of N paired multi-modal observations C = { c (1) , c (2) , . . . , c ( N ) } , where each cell c ( i ) = ( x ( i ) , y ( i ) ) consists of an ATAC-seq profile x ( i ) and its matched RNA-seq profile y ( i ). In addition, each cell c ( i ) is associated with a semantic label ℓ ( i ) ∈ { 1 , . . . , T } indicating its cell type among T classes. For a given cell type T = k , we denote by C k the subset of C containing all cells whose labels satisfy ℓ ( i ) = k .

GRIDS: Learnable Subset Perturbations for Global Regulatory Redundancy Reasoning
5.3 Methods
5.3.1 Problem Setup
Following the formulation in Wu et al. [273], we represent the cis-regulatory landscape of a cell by an ATAC-seq vector x ∈ { 0 , 1 } d a , where each entry corresponds to the accessibility state of a genomic peak (1 for open and 0 for closed). In practice, ATAC-seq profiles are extremely high-dimensional, typically with d a > 10 5 . The corresponding gene expression measurements (RNA-seq) are denoted by a real-valued vector y ∈ R d r , where d a and d r indicate the numbers of peaks and genes, respectively.
Asingle-cell multi-omics dataset is given as a collection of N paired multi-modal observations C = { c (1) , c (2) , . . . , c ( N ) } , where each cell c ( i ) = ( x ( i ) , y ( i ) ) consists of an ATAC-seq profile x ( i ) and its matched RNA-seq profile y ( i ). In addition, each cell c ( i ) is associated with a semantic label ℓ ( i ) ∈ { 1 , . . . , T } indicating its cell type among T classes. For a given cell type T = k , we denote by C k the subset of C containing all cells whose labels satisfy ℓ ( i ) = k .
As introduced above, gene expression is regulated through CRE-mediated transcriptional control implemented by complex intracellular processes. We abstract this relationship using a regulatory function y = F ( x ), where F ( x ) : R d a → R d r . Because F corresponds to an underlying biological mechanism, it is costly to query directly and is treated as a black box. The regulatory redundancy dissection problem then aims to identify a subset of L peak indices r = { r 1 , . . . , r L } within the CRE space (i.e., the subset feature in the ATAC-seq x r ≡ { x j | j ∈ r } ) that are crucial for controlling a target gene's expression over a population of cells. The search domain of r is the binomial subset space ( d a L ) , which is prohibitively large given that x typically contains more than 10 5 dimensions.
To make this problem tractable, we model redundancy dissection within a global feature explanation framework. In general, global explanations quantify how much a model's performance degrades over a sample population when selected features are removed [46]. where L measures the expected degradation in gene expression. Here, x \ r denotes the perturbed CRE representation induced by r , obtained by replacing the original features x r j with preset perturbation values p ∈ R d a at the indices specified by r (i.e., x \ r,r j = p r j ). When p = 0, this reduces to a removal-based perturbation. The specific form of the loss depends on the model and task [63]; for instance, cross-entropy is commonly used to measure probability degradation in classification, whereas in our setting we adopt a mean-squared loss to quantify degradation of gene expression values.
